title: The big lookout
hook: year one ends: look back down the hill, then up

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stoa, and the ranges ahead. Your line was the ranges. Did you find the farthest thing you could see, and let it be far? Day three hundred thirty-one. The last day of year one.

At the top of the hill there's a lookout. A flat rock, a rail, maybe a bench someone carved their initials into. This is day three hundred thirty-one of the climb. Maybe some days you ran. Maybe some you crawled. Maybe on a few you sat down on the path and didn't move, and that counted too. Now you're here. Below you, the whole trail, switchbacks and all, back down to the spot where you took one breath with a bell. Above and beyond, the ranges. You get to stand in the middle, for one day, and see both. Today: the big lookout.
screen: `A FLAT ROCK, A RAIL, A BENCH.` → `331 DAYS OF CLIMBING.` → `THE TRAIL BELOW, THE RANGES BEYOND.`

segments.voice: First, look down at the camps. The first words, starting with breathe. The stories: a shipwreck, a butterfly, a carob tree. The practices: the breath, the evening review, the sunset. The text: Rumi's reed, with Marcus beside him. Second, look down at this last camp, the depths, the longest of all. We went as guests into seven homes. Hinduism: dharma, and you are that. Buddhism: wake up, and may all beings be well. Judaism: hear, and repair. Christianity: love your neighbor, and grace. The Catholic tradition: the rosary and the works of mercy. Islam: one God, and hearts that find rest in remembrance. Sikhism: the name, honest work, and the free kitchen. Then home to the Stoic porch: character, the four virtues, the citadel. Then the lab: resonance breathing, sixty-six days, take it for a walk somewhere green, he giveth his beloved sleep, and Hume's gap between is and ought. Third, a line from a tradition that loved hills. A psalm, in the King James words: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." The next verse answers: the help comes from God, the maker of heaven and earth. The King James Bible heads this psalm a song of degrees, and tradition links those songs with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Fourth, a line from the Tao Te Ching, in James Legge's translation: "The journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step." You took that step on day one. Every step since was also a single step. That's all a year is. Look how far. Tomorrow, the porch: year two opens with a little handbook meant to be kept at hand.
screen: `WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, THE TEXT.` · `SEVEN HOMES, THE PORCH, THE LAB.` · `I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.` · `A THOUSAND LI, A SINGLE STEP.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Stand somewhere high, if you can: a hill, a balcony, the top of the stairs. Or go to a window. First, look down. Let the year pass below you: a face, a story, a hard week, a good one. Then take one breath, the same breath as day one. Now look up, at the sky above you. Stay there, between the trail below and the open sky. The bell holds the time.
Rumi, whose reed appears at the big lookout, the top of year one: look back down the whole trail, then up at the ranges. Today's word, and the last of the year.
Your line: look how far. Tell one person tonight that you finished a year of this. Then rest. Tomorrow, the porch. Day three hundred thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 331 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HANDBOOK FOR THE ROAD.`

howItsDone: Many people mark the end of a long stretch of practice by going somewhere high or open, looking back over what they did, and naming what comes next.

fork.setup: you're at the lookout at the end of year one. where do you look?
options: only back, at what you missed.
down at the trail, then up at the ranges.
only ahead, at what's still left.
fork.reveal: the lookout is for both: look how far you came, then look up. tomorrow, year two begins.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the course.
what it means: the top of year one, where you see the whole trail and the ranges beyond.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 121, a song of ascents, traditionally linked with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, and Tao Te Ching 64 on the single step.

notes: Psalm 121:1 KJV: confirm exact wording. Readers differ on whether 'from whence cometh my help' is a question (many modern translations) or a statement (KJV punctuation); the script keeps the KJV and adds verse 2's answer in paraphrase.

Tao Te Ching 64, Legge 1891 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 39): checked against the Project Gutenberg Legge text, which reads 'commenced' (past tense), not 'commences'. Fixed in voice, myth and source.

Editor review 2026-10-01: corrected the Legge quotation ('commences' was not Legge's wording); replaced the banned 'Picture' hook opener and the lines telling listeners what they did ('some of them you ran') with 'maybe'; cut the sweeping 'hills are where people have always gone to look up' and grounded the pilgrimage note in the KJV heading 'A Song of degrees' plus 'tradition links'; changed the practice's last step to the sky so it no longer repeats day 330's look-to-the-horizon practice.
Camp 5 recap lists the visit weeks' carries (days 232–280), the Stoic weeks (281–301) and the science weeks (302–324). Confirm 'hearts that find rest in remembrance' matches day 269.
Psalm 121 as a song of ascents associated with pilgrimage: traditional reading; confirm.
Year close and Camp 5 close; tomorrow opens Year Two with day 332, 'The handbook for the road'.
